segments.title: Opening, name and birth in Greenville, Mississippi
segments.summary: Recording starts; Jones gives his name, birth date (1874) and birthplace.

segments.title: Early years in the Mississippi valley states, no attention to music
segments.summary: He lived at home until 16, then worked in Arkansas, Missouri, Illinois and Tennessee, paying no attention to music until he came to New Orleans. An interviewer aside clarifies they want the Bolden period.

segments.title: Moving to New Orleans in 1894 and the ragtime music he found
segments.summary: He came to New Orleans in January 1894; the music was rag, with Peyton the accordion player downtown and Bolden coming up after learning from Manuel Hall.

segments.title: Peyton's string band and where it played
segments.summary: Peyton was older than Bolden and led a string band with fiddle, trombone and accordion, playing at the 25s near Custom House and Franklin.

segments.title: Peyton compared with Bolden: ragtime and blues
segments.summary: Peyton was a famous accordion player who also played blues but did not become famous for it as Bolden did.

segments.title: Young Bolden, Manuel Hall and playing by ear
segments.summary: When Jones arrived Bolden was just learning, with no band; Manuel Hall broke him in. Bolden could hear a band at the theater and play the piece at the dance that night.

segments.title: Where Bolden grew up on First Street; his real name
segments.summary: Bolden grew up on First Street between Liberty and Howard; the interviewers' city directory lists Charles Bowen, which Jones confirms as his right name.

segments.title: Bolden had no other job; Jones's barbering and blindness
segments.summary: Bolden only played music after school, never barbered. Jones was a barber himself, stopped about 20 years ago and lost his sight.

segments.title: Finding others who knew Bolden; his fame after 1900
segments.summary: Jones thinks everyone who knew Bolden is dead; Bolden became really famous after 1900.

segments.title: Members of Bolden's band: Mumford, bass player, Cornish
segments.summary: Jones recalls Mumford (guitar, nicknamed Brock), a bass player named Jimmy, and Willie Cornish, Bolden's trombone player, and suggests looking in the Cherokee and Ann neighborhood.

segments.title: When Bolden formed his band and Manuel Hall's role
segments.summary: Bolden started his own band around 1900, called Bolden's Band. Manuel Hall had no band of his own.

segments.title: How Bolden differed from earlier reading bands
segments.summary: Earlier bands were all readers; Bolden could hear a piece and have his band playing it by daylight.

segments.title: Halls and parks where Bolden played
segments.summary: Jones names Masonic Hall, Valley Hall, Jackson Street Hall, St. Elizabeth Hall, Lincoln Park, Johnson Park and Providence Hall, and tells of Bolden calling his children home from Johnson Park.

segments.title: Bolden played only dance jobs; other parade bands
segments.summary: Bolden's was always a dance band, never seen on the street; Jones vaguely recalls the Excelsior and other club parade bands.

segments.title: Tunes and dances in Bolden's time
segments.summary: Jones recalls Funky Butt, waltzes, mazurkas and quadrilles, knows nothing of slow drag, and cannot say whether Careless Love or Buckets Got a Hole in It were played.

segments.title: Audiences, dancing and admission price
segments.summary: Most people danced; Jones listened rather than danced. Admission was twenty-five to forty cents.

segments.title: End of Bolden's career and what became of the band
segments.summary: Bolden stopped playing a couple of years before losing his mind and being taken to Jackson, dying around 1909. Jones does not know who led the band afterward; he remembers Frankie Dusen as a player.

segments.title: Asking about other musicians: Warner, Lewis, Klim, the Franks
segments.summary: Interviewers ask about Willie Warner, Frank Lewis, Baltimore, Edward Klim and the Frank brothers; Jones remembers few, with Klim a good clarinetist less of a rag player than Bolden. Jones's wife says the questioning is puzzling him.

segments.title: Church, religion and hymns
segments.summary: Asked whether Bolden's family went to church, Jones cannot answer; he says he was raised Baptist but does not sing and recalls no hymns. The transcript has garbled repetition here.

segments.title: Bolden's sister Cora, his children and their mothers
segments.summary: Bolden had an older sister Cora, never married, had a daughter by a woman named Nora (Laura Bass), and Jones believes a son whose mother was Hattie.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: The interviewers thank Jones and let the tape run out.
